transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what’s been going on that brought you in today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, thanks for fitting me in. I, um... well, it's getting to the point where I'm just losing hours of my day, every single day, to rechecking things. And I know how that sounds, but it's not just double-checking to be safe. I'm an engineer, I graduated a couple years ago, so obviously I'm used to being precise and paying attention to details, but this is entirely different. I get completely stuck. 

It happens with all sorts of things, honestly. Like my dressing supplies in the morning, making sure they are exactly how they need to be, or the door locks before I leave my apartment. I'll stand at the front door and check the deadbolt, but then I have to do it again, and again, because it just doesn't feel right. And it bleeds into my work, too, which is really stressing me out. I'll be looking at file dimensions on my computer, or going through my revision notes for a project, and I’ll just get caught in this loop. I know I just looked at the numbers, but I don’t feel... allowed to move on. That's the best way I can describe it. 

It’s like my brain won't give me permission to switch tasks or leave the room until I’ve gone through the exact same checking routine enough times. If I try to just force myself to walk away, this massive wave of anxiety hits me, and I can't focus on anything else anyway because I'm just thinking about what I didn't check. So I have to keep doing the routine, over and over, until it finally clicks and the anxiety drops enough for me to actually breathe and move on to the next thing. It's just completely exhausting and it's eating up my whole life right now.

Can you tell me if these checking routines are connected to a specific worry or thought that keeps coming into your mind, or do they feel more like something you just have to do even if you’re not sure why?

Yeah, it’s... it's definitely a specific worry. It's not just a random urge where my body moves on its own, it’s actually driven by these very specific, really intense thoughts, and they're always catastrophic. 

Like, for example, with the dressing supplies I mentioned—I have this minor thing I've been managing, and I'll go through the whole process. I'll wash my hands, prep everything, do it all by the book. But even after I *know* for an absolute fact that I’ve cleaned the wound area perfectly, this... this thought just cuts right in. It just pierces through whatever else I'm thinking, and it tells me that I missed one tiny thing. Just one microscopic spot or one little misstep. And then it spirals, and my brain is suddenly convinced that this tiny mistake is going to turn into some massive, horrible infection. 

And it's the exact same mechanism at work, which is why my days are getting so incredibly long. I’ll be reviewing a CAD file—I work with a lot of structural designs, so precision is obviously part of the job—but I'll have reviewed it completely, checked all the parameters, and then that same kind of thought barges in. "What if you missed a tolerance? What if one dimension is off by a fraction?" And it instantly turns into this vivid, overwhelming fear that it’s going to turn into a design mistake that actually hurts someone. Like, a piece of equipment failing and physically injuring a person, and it would be entirely my fault because I missed that one tiny thing. 

And the most frustrating part—the part that makes me feel like I'm losing my mind—is that I can't just reason it away. I try! I really do. I sit there and try to use logic, like, "You're an engineer, you literally just looked at the screen, the numbers are right there, it's mathematically sound." But the logic doesn't even make a dent. It’s like the rational part of my brain gets completely hijacked, and no amount of reasoning can convince me that someone isn't going to get hurt or I'm not going to get sick. The thought just stays there, completely blocking me from moving on, until I finally give in and check it again.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms, including intrusive catastrophic thoughts related to specific worries (e.g., infection, design errors), repetitive checking behaviors aimed at reducing anxiety, and the inability to dismiss the thoughts through logic, strongly point toward OCD. The presence of both obsessions (unwanted, intrusive thoughts) and compulsions (repetitive checking behaviors) is consistent with F42.2 (Obsessive-compulsive disorder). Other candidates (e.g., depressive or anxiety disorders without obsessions/compulsions) are less consistent with the clinical presentation described so far.

inference_history.note: The patient presents with symptoms of persistent, intrusive thoughts and repetitive, ritualistic behaviors that cause significant distress and impairment in daily functioning. This suggests a primary consideration for obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42.2). Other candidates include adjustment disorder (F43.20), generalized anxiety disorder (F43.00), post-traumatic stress disorder (F43.10), major depressive disorder (F32.0–F32.3), and other specified anxiety or obsessive-compulsive and related disorders (F06.4, F06.89). Further questioning is needed to rule in or out specific diagnoses.
